brief: Shanghai crude futures broke above $100/bbl and swung from a spread as negative as -$20 versus Brent in April to a premium as high as $25, a signal the piece frames as behind Brent's rise to $101.61 (up about 36% since the US-Iran war started in late February) before the spread collapsed back to flat. Goldman says this was not a China demand rebound: high-frequency seaborne imports rose only 6% (0.5mb/d) in September and stayed nearly 3mb/d below seasonal norms at 7.2mb/d, 27% below a year ago. What changed is composition: Russian and Iranian crude fell from about half of China's imports in August to under a third in September as a US blockade curbed Iranian exports and attacks on Russian ports continued, pushing refiners into the open market and supporting Brent/WTI. Two Goldman models, a supply-demand balance and a price-lagged regression, both put China's imports near August levels into October, with domestic demand still weak (gasoline/diesel consumption down 9% YoY). Because the market has already priced in a bigger China rebound, Goldman expects Brent to edge lower absent Mideast escalation, which it calls the actual upside risk to its base case of $80 Brent in 2027.
